overview.body:
**Hoori** ​(*hoori*) ‌— Agriculture, ‌Hunter ​— ​belongs to ​the ​Japanese ​tradition. The ‌name ​means ​"Fire-subduing"[^1].

Hoori ‌is ​the ‌younger ​son of ‌Ninigi, ​the ​hunter whose ​marriage ​to ​the sea ‌princess ​Toyotama ‌produces the ​imperial ‌line.

​PuniCodex ‌restores the ​name ‌as ​**Hoori**. The ​plain ‌ASCII ‌form *hoori* ‌is ​the ​modern Hepburn ‌romanization; ​the ​restoration ‌capitalizes the ​conventional ​spelling. ‌Because the ​Japanese ‌source ​script uses ​logographic ​characters ​whose ‌distinctive visual ‌form ​cannot ‌be conveyed ​in ​the ‌basic Latin ‌alphabet, ‌and ‌because no ​diacritic ‌or ​special ​letter is ​added ‌in ​this restoration, ​the ​name ‌is placed ​in ​Tier ​2. The ‌Unicode ​form ‌remains ​the philologically ‌complete ​reference, ‌while the ‌ASCII ​spelling ​is a ​practical ​convenience ‌for the ‌domain-name ​system[^2].

the-name.body:
The ​name is ‌attested in ‌Japanese characters ​as **火折命**. ​Etymologically it ​means "Fire-subduing"[^1].

​Hoori's name ​means "fire-subduing" ‌or "fire-bending," ​from *ho* ​(fire) and ‌*ori* (to ​bend, subdue). ‌He is ​the younger ‌son of ​Ninigi and ​the ancestor ​of the ​imperial line ​through his ‌son Ugayafukiaezu ​and grandson ‌Jimmu. His ​marriage to ‌Toyotama, daughter ​of the ‌sea god ​Ryūjin, is ‌one of ​the great ​mythic romances ‌of the ‌*Kojiki*.

The ‌ASCII form ​*hoori* survives ​only because ‌the early ​domain-name system ​could not ‌carry Japanese ​characters or ​diacritics; it ‌is a ​technological compromise, ‌not an ​ancient spelling. ​The Unicode ​restoration **Hoori** ​gives the ‌conventional Hepburn ‌romanization with ​initial capitalization, ‌the standard ​scholarly way ​to cite ‌a proper ‌name in ‌romanized Japanese. ‌The name ​is Tier ‌2 because ​the restoration ​does not ​add a ‌distinctive diacritic ​or special ​letter absent ​from the ‌ASCII form.

​The letter-by-letter ​transformation runs:

​- **h** ‌→ **H** ​— Same, ‌capitalized
- ​**o** → ‌**o** — ​Same
- ‌**o** → ‌**o** — ​Same
- ​**r** → ​**r** — ​Same
- ‌**i** → ‌**i** — ​Same

pronunciation.body:
The conventional ​reading of ‌the name ‌is **/hoː.ɾi/** ​— Modern ​Japanese (Standard ​Japanese)[^1].

For ​the modern speaker, ​the closest ‌approximation is: ​'HOORI' — ​pronounce each ‌vowel clearly ​and avoid ‌English diphthongs. Japanese ​is mora-timed, ‌so each ​syllable receives ​roughly equal ​weight.



Hoori ​is Tier 2 ​because the ‌ASCII form ​*hoori* already ‌represents the ​same phonemic ‌sequence; no ​stress mark, length ‌mark, or ​distinctive letter ‌is required ​to recover ​the spoken ‌name.

Japanese ‌is a mora-timed ‌language: each ​short syllable ​receives roughly ‌equal temporal ​weight, and ​long vowels ‌or double consonants ​count as ​separate morae. ‌The name ​**Hoori** therefore ‌falls into ​a regular rhythmic ​pattern that ​is lost ​if an ‌English speaker ‌stresses one ​syllable heavily[^2]. ‌The Hepburn romanization ​used here ​records the ‌modern standard ‌pronunciation; it ‌does not ‌preserve the ​historical pitch accent ‌of the ​word, which ​differs across ​dialects. When ‌reading the ​name aloud, ​keep the vowels ​pure and ‌avoid English ​diphthongs: the ​restoration **Hoori** ​is the ‌conventional scholarly citation ​form, not ‌a phonetic ​transcription with ‌added diacritics. ​Because the ‌ASCII string ‌*hoori* already encodes ​the same ​phonemic sequence, ​the name ​remains Tier ‌2 in ‌the PuniCodex ​system.

sources.citation: Hepburn, James Curtis, A Japanese-English and English-Japanese Dictionary, 1867.

domains.body:
Hoori ​is the ‌hunter and ‌the ​ancestor of ​rulers. His ​domain ​is the ​land, the ‌bow, ​and the ​legitimate succession ‌from ​heaven to ‌earth. Through ​his ‌descent to ​the sea ​palace ​and his ​marriage to ​Toyotama, ‌he also ​bridges the ‌terrestrial ​and marine ‌worlds, establishing ​the ‌imperial line ​as mediators ‌between ​both.

The ​domain of ‌**Hoori** ‌is understood ‌within the ​broader ​Japanese religious ‌landscape as ​both ​a specific ‌functional sphere ​and ​a node ‌in a ​network of ‌kami, ​buddhas, and ​local spirits. ​Shrines, ​temples, and ‌household rites ‌all ​invoke the ‌figure in ​ways ​that blur ‌strict boundaries ‌between ‌Shinto and ‌Buddhist practice[^3]. ​The ‌restoration **Hoori** ​therefore names ​not ​only a ‌mythic person ​but ​a living ​field of ‌ritual ​activity: pilgrimage, ​festival, iconography, ​and ‌prayer continue ​to define ‌what ​the name ‌means in ​contemporary ‌Japan. This ‌combinatory or ​"syncretic" ​context is ​essential for ​interpreting ‌the domains ‌listed above.
​

sources.citation: Breen, John, and Mark Teeuwen, A New History of Shinto (Wiley-Blackwell, 2010).

mythology.body:
Hoori married ​Toyotama, daughter ‌of the ‌sea god ​Ryūjin, at ​the bottom ​of the ​sea. She ​made him ‌promise not ​to watch ​her give ‌birth, but ​he broke ‌the promise ​and saw ‌her in ​the form ​of a giant ​crocodile or ​sea dragon. ​Ashamed, she ‌returned to ​the sea, ‌leaving her ​sister Tamayori ‌to raise ​the child ‌Ugayafukiaezu. The ​recovered fish ‌hook, the ​tide jewels, ​and the ‌sea-god's blessing ‌enabled Hoori ‌to subdue his ​elder brother ​Hoderi and ‌establish the ​line that ​would produce ‌the first ​emperor Jimmu.

​The narrative ‌of **Hoori** ​participates in ‌the larger ​mythic program ​of the ​*Kojiki* and ​*Nihon Shoki*: ‌to explain ‌the origins ​of the imperial ‌house, the ​division of ​divine labour, ‌and the ‌relationship between ‌the human ‌and kami ​worlds. Because ‌these chronicles ​were compiled ​in the ​eighth century ‌under imperial ​patronage, the ​myths also ​serve a ‌political theology, grounding ​earthly authority ​in divine ​descent and ‌cosmic order[^3]. ​Read comparatively, ‌the story ​of hoori ‌illustrates how ​Japanese myth ‌uses genealogy, ‌descent from ​heaven, and ​the negotiation ​of rival ​domains to ‌construct a ‌coherent sacred ​history.

kojiki-nihonshoki.body:
The ​*Kojiki* and ‌*Nihon Shoki* ‌are ​the earliest ​written witnesses ​to **Hoori**, ​although ​the figure ‌may have ​circulated ​in oral ‌and local ​cult forms ‌long ​before the ‌eighth century. ​In ​the chronicles, ​Hoori appears ​as ​the younger ‌son of ​Ninigi, husband ‌of ​Toyotama, and ‌forefather of ​Emperor ‌Jimmu, embedded ​in the ‌imperial ​genealogy and ​the narrative ‌of cosmic ‌order[^1]. ‌The *Kojiki* ​account tends ​to ‌privilege the ​mythic lineage ​leading to ‌Amaterasu ​and the ​imperial house, ‌while ​the *Nihon ‌Shoki* often ​presents ​variant traditions ​side by ​side, preserving ‌conflicting ‌genealogies and ​episodes.

Because ‌both ​texts were ​compiled under ‌imperial patronage, ‌their ‌portrayal of ‌Hoori is ​never ‌purely "mythological" ​in a ​neutral ​sense; it ‌is also ​a statement ​about ​legitimacy, territory, ‌and the ​proper ​ordering of ​the human ‌and ​divine worlds[^2]. ‌Modern readers ​must therefore ‌distinguish ​between the ‌older narrative ‌strata ​preserved in ​the chronicles ​and the ​ideological ‌framing imposed ‌by the ​compilers.

shinto-sources.body:
Beyond ​the *Kojiki* ‌and ‌*Nihon ​Shoki*, the ​Shinto ​sources for ​**Hoori** ​include shrine ‌records ​(*engi*), ​ritual prayers ‌(*norito*), ​imperial ritual ‌protocols, ​and the ‌vast ​corpus ​of local ​festival ​traditions preserved ​at ‌shrines ​across Japan[^1]. ‌These ​documents reveal ‌how ​a figure ‌who ​begins ‌as a ​line ​in an ‌imperial ‌chronicle becomes ‌the ​focus ​of pilgrimage, ‌divination, ​and community ​identity. ‌The ​*Fudoki*, or ​provincial ‌gazetteers, add ​topographical ‌and etymological ​details ​that ​connect Hoori ​to ‌specific mountains, ‌rivers, ​and ‌villages.

Medieval ​and ​early-modern Shinto ‌texts ‌also reinterpret ‌Hoori ‌in ​light of ‌Buddhist, ​Confucian, and ​nativist ​agendas. The ‌early-modern ​*kokugaku* ​(National Learning) ​scholars, ‌in particular, ​sought ​to ​recover a ‌pure ​Shinto reading ‌of ​the figure, ‌stripped ​of ‌Buddhist accretions[^2]. ‌Their ​interpretations remain ​influential ​in contemporary ​shrine ‌theology ‌and popular ​understanding.

sources.citation: Ono, Sokyo, Shinto: The Kami Way (Tuttle, 1962).
Breen, John, and Mark Teeuwen, A New History of Shinto (Wiley-Blackwell, 2010).

buddhist-japanese.body:
Japanese ​Buddhist ‌sources treat ‌**Hoori** ​through ​the lens ​of ​*honji-suijaku*, ​the theory ‌that ​local ​kami are ‌traces ​or ‌manifestations of ​universal ‌Buddhist ​truths. Medieval ​temple-shrine ​complexes ​produced rituals, ​images, ‌and ​narratives ‌that identified ​Hoori ‌with ​a Buddhist ‌counterpart, ​integrating ‌the figure ​into ​esoteric ‌mandalas, Pure ‌Land ‌devotion, ​and warrior ​protector ‌cults[^1]. ​These identifications ​were ‌not ​merely symbolic; ​they ‌reorganized ​the ‌ritual calendar, ​patronage ​networks, ​and sacred ​geography ‌of ‌the sites ​involved.

‌The ​Meiji-era policy ​of ‌*shinbutsu ‌bunri* formally ‌separated ‌kami ​and buddhas, ‌but ​Buddhist ​elements survived ​in ‌architecture, ​festival ​customs, and ​popular ‌iconography. ​Modern scholarship ​therefore ​reads ‌Hoori through ​both ‌Shinto ​and Buddhist ‌archives, ​recognizing ‌that the ‌two ​traditions ​shaped each ​other ​for ‌more than ‌a ​millennium[^2].
